response.answer: Deploying LLM-based mental health tools in low-resource clinics requires balancing high operational costs and compute demands with limited infrastructure, often opting for locally run, less powerful models to minimize costs. Model selection should prioritize ethical standards and equity, while maintenance focuses on local, sustainable solutions.

results.title: JMIR Mental Health - The Opportunities and Risks of Large Language Models in Mental Health
results.content: Global rates of mental health concerns are rising, and there is increasing realization that existing models of mental health care will not adequately expand to meet the demand. In this paper, we summarize the extant literature on efforts to use LLMs to provide mental health education, assessment, and intervention and highlight key opportunities for positive impact in each area. The urgent need for mental health support must be balanced with responsible development, testing, and deployment of mental health LLMs. It is especially critical to ensure that mental health LLMs are fine-tuned for mental health, enhance mental health equity, and adhere to ethical standards and that people, including those with lived experience with mental health concerns, are involved in all stages from development through deployment. The emergence of large language models (LLMs) brings hope regarding their application to mental health and their potential to provide such solutions due to their relevance to mental health education, assessment, and intervention.

results.title: Frontiers | Synthetic patient and interview transcript creator: an essential tool for LLMs in mental health
results.content: # Synthetic patient and interview transcript creator: an essential tool for LLMs in mental health. To address privacy and legal constraints associated with real patient data, we designed a synthetic patient and interview generation framework that can be tailored to regional patient demographics. This system employs two locally run instances of Llama 3.3:70B: one as the interviewer and the other as the patient. We calculate median Distinct-1 scores of 0.44 and 0.33 for the patient and interview assistant model outputs respectively compared to 0.50 ± 0.11 as the average for 10,000 episodes of a radio program dialog. Central to this approach is the patient generation process, which begins with a locally run Llama 3.3:70B model. Given the full question bank, the model generates a detailed profile template, combining predefined variables (e.g., demographic data or specific conditions) with LLM-generated content to fill in contextual details. To address this, we present a synthetic patient and interview generation framework that leverages two instances of Llama 3.3 70B models.
